clue.text: Apt reading Bond created

indicators.note: created means made up or fashioned, so the preceding letters are shaped into something new

explanation.surface: A fitting text for reading, made by an author called Bond.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of APT READING BOND, signalled by 'created', gives the answer, and the whole clue also defines it: Michael Bond wrote the stories of this bear, named after the London railway station where he is found.
explanation.definitionFit: Michael Bond was the author who invented the marmalade-loving bear from Peru.

clue.text: All the cops in new uniform? Wrong!

indicators.note: new means made afresh, so these letters are formed into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone guesses that every officer has been issued new kit, and is told that is not so.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges ALL THE COPS IN. The definition is a uniform that is wrong: detectives dress like ordinary people, the opposite of police uniform.
explanation.definitionFit: Ordinary dress worn by detectives is the reverse of the regulation outfit, so a wrong kind of uniform.

clue.text: Outline for military service?

definitions.meaning: a first rough version or sketch of a plan or text
in the US, compulsory conscription into the armed forces

explanation.surface: Someone asks for a sketch of what serving in the army involves.
explanation.definitionFit: A preliminary sketch is a rough version; conscription in America is also known by this word.

clue.text: Topless Italian has to tickle bottomless numskull

indicators.note: topless means losing the top, so the first letter of the word is removed

parts.note: Signor is the Italian title for a man, so an Italian gentleman

indicators.note: bottomless means the bottom, the final letter of this down word, is dropped

parts.note: to tickle someone can mean to amuse them

explanation.surface: A semi-naked Italian is told to tickle a foolish person with no bottom on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' strips S from SIGNOR, leaving IGNOR; 'bottomless' strips E from AMUSE, leaving AMUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe an ignorant, stupid person.

clue.text: First of the girls with simply tailored tunic

indicators.note: First of means only the opening letter of the next word is taken
tailored means cut and shaped, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A schoolgirl's tunic described as plainly cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tailored' looks like it describes the tunic, but it is the anagram signal. A gymslip is a sleeveless pinafore once standard in British girls' school uniform.
explanation.definitionFit: A sleeveless pinafore dress once worn by British schoolgirls, so a kind of tunic.

clue.text: Work in a supervisory role, like a bishop?

definitions.meaning: to supervise or watch over others' work
read as two words, a bishop is 'over' his see, the diocese he governs

explanation.surface: A job description for a manager, compared to a churchman's position.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as OVER SEE: a see is a bishop's diocese, and he sits over it.
explanation.definitionFit: To supervise is to watch over and direct the work of others.

clue.text: It's terrible about half of lake having dried out

indicators.note: about means going around, so the outer word wraps the other piece
half of takes the back half of the word lake

explanation.surface: A lake has dried up, half of it gone, and that is terrible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half of' takes the back half of 'lake', and 'about' wraps the terrible word round it.
explanation.definitionFit: Earth or clay that has been baked has been hardened and parched by heat.

clue.text: Take choir trip to Jerusalem, say

indicators.note: to trip is to stumble, so the letters fall into a new order

explanation.surface: An instruction to take a church choir on a tour of Jerusalem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jerusalem' looks like the destination of the trip, but it is the definition: a Jerusalem artichoke is a vegetable.
explanation.definitionFit: The Jerusalem artichoke is a knobbly root vegetable, an example of this plant name.

clue.text: Cooking range that's popular once more

parts.note: an Aga is a brand of heavy cast-iron range cooker common in British country kitchens

explanation.surface: A kitchen stove that has come back into fashion.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something a second time is doing it anew, which is what this adverb means.

clue.text: Aleksandr, Sergei and Oleg are just pets, I hear

indicators.note: I hear says the words are recognised by their sound, not their spelling

parts.note: just means mere, and cats are pets, giving 'mere cats'

explanation.surface: Three Russian men turn out to be nothing more than household animals.
explanation.walkthrough: Aleksandr, Sergei and Oleg are the animated characters in the British adverts for the price-comparison site comparethemarket.com.
explanation.definitionFit: The three are animated mongoose-family animals from television adverts, so examples of this species.

clue.text: Brother who keeps mum

parts.note: a monk of an order famous for its rule of silence, so a brother who keeps quiet rather than caring for his mother

explanation.surface: A sibling who looks after his mother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeps mum' suggests looking after Mother, but it means staying silent; 'Brother' is a monk.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of this Cistercian order are known for living by a vow of silence.

clue.text: Someone sure to succeed but isn't sharp

definitions.meaning: a person with an inborn talent who is bound to do well
in music, a note that is neither sharp nor flat

explanation.surface: A paradox: a person bound to do well who is not especially clever.
explanation.definitionFit: A gifted person is a born talent; in music notation the sign cancelling a sharp has the same name.

clue.text: Cocktail attachment

definitions.meaning: a drink of brandy, orange liqueur and lemon juice
a passenger car attached to the side of a motorcycle

explanation.surface: An extra piece fitted to a mixed drink.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both a classic brandy drink and the passenger pod bolted beside a motorbike.

clue.text: Sub edited unfinished column

indicators.note: edited means revised and rearranged, so the letters are reordered
unfinished means the last letter of the word is cut off

explanation.surface: A sub-editor has reworked a newspaper column that was left incomplete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfinished' drops N from COLUMN, and 'edited' rearranges the remaining COLUM. 'Sub' looks like a sub-editor but means a stand-in.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctor or cleric who stands in for another is a substitute, shortened to sub.

clue.text: Medicare provision originally organised — it's now or never!

indicators.note: organised means put in order, so the letters are rearranged
originally means at the origin, so only the first letter is taken

explanation.surface: A US health scheme has been set up and must be grabbed while it is available.
explanation.walkthrough: 'originally' takes P from 'provision', and 'organised' rearranges MEDICARE plus P.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin motto means seize the day, urging action at once before the chance passes.

clue.text: Classmates or upper-class mates?

definitions.meaning: people of the same age or status, such as schoolfellows
a gathering of peers, that is lords, read literally

explanation.surface: A question whether one's fellow pupils are aristocratic friends.
explanation.definitionFit: One's equals in age or status form this social set; peers are also nobles.

clue.text: Deteriorates, as a user may

definitions.meaning: a drug user may take to cannabis, known as pot

explanation.surface: Something gets worse, in the way a consumer might.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes something falling into decay; literally a drug user heads towards cannabis.

clue.text: Wader changes colour

parts.note: a tone is a shade of colour

explanation.surface: Someone paddling has gone a different colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wader' looks like a person paddling, but it is a shore bird.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a small shore bird that flips over pebbles looking for food.

clue.text: Isolated rock from Route 51

indicators.note: from here means the answer is made out of these letters, rearranged

explanation.surface: A lone boulder found along a numbered highway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' signals that ROUTE and LI are mixed up to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: In geology, younger rock left detached from the main formation by erosion is called this.

clue.text: Time for ironing?

definitions.meaning: the part of the day after afternoon

explanation.surface: A question asking when the pressing of clothes gets done.
explanation.definitionFit: Late in the day before night is one sense; smoothing creases makes things even.

clue.text: Earth and lime mixture providing resin

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for earth, as on electrical plugs

indicators.note: a mixture is a stirred blend, so the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A recipe: blend soil and lime to make a gum.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a fragrant gum from tropical trees used in varnishes and ointments.

clue.text: Graceful and neat, oddly concealing limb

indicators.note: concealing means hiding inside, so the outer letters wrap the next piece
oddly means in a strange way, so the letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A dancer who is graceful and tidy hides a leg in an unusual way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' looks like a pick of odd letters but is the anagram signal, making EANT; 'concealing' puts the limb inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Both describe stylish poise and refinement of movement or appearance.

clue.text: Backer on the Tube?

definitions.meaning: a financial backer of a theatre production
A station on the London Underground, known as the Tube

explanation.surface: A sponsor seen riding the London Underground.
explanation.definitionFit: An investor in a show is called this in theatre slang; it is also a Northern line station.

clue.text: Novice competitor

definitions.meaning: someone just entering a profession or field
someone who enters a race or contest

explanation.surface: A beginner taking part in a contest.
explanation.definitionFit: A newcomer to a field and a person signed up for a contest both share this word.

clue.text: Calls on head regularly for welcome

indicators.note: regularly means at regular intervals, so every second letter is picked

explanation.surface: Someone pays frequent visits to the boss to be greeted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes the 2nd, 4th, 6th, 8th and 10th letters of CALLS ON HEAD.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hawaiian word is used as a greeting of hello as well as goodbye.

clue.text: Cook lining up initially one type of pasta

indicators.note: to cook can mean to fiddle or falsify, so the letters are reworked
initially means at the start, so only the first letter is taken

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A recipe instruction: cook one kind of pasta after lining it up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cook' rearranges LINING plus U (from 'up initially') into LINGUIN, and I for 'one' ends it.
explanation.definitionFit: These are long flat ribbons of Italian noodle, narrower than fettuccine.

clue.text: Publicity for Farah?

parts.note: Mo Farah is the British Olympic long-distance running champion

explanation.surface: Asking about press coverage for a famous runner.
explanation.definitionFit: A short promotional video or advert is a piece of publicity.

clue.text: Self-centred response from Jill after fall

definitions.text: Self-centred response from Jill after fall

parts.words: Self-centred response from Jill after fall
parts.note: a phrase expressing selfish indifference to others, imagined as Jill's reply after the nursery rhyme fall, where Jack broke his crown

explanation.surface: Jill's selfish words after tumbling down the hill.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme Jack and Jill, Jack falls and breaks his crown and Jill comes tumbling after; she now tells Jack she is fine.
explanation.definitionFit: The British catchphrase expresses smug selfishness, being content oneself regardless of others.
